commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Fill in programming and IDE experience
Chatbot: Rename to Rocky, add greet and exit
Echo user input, exit on bye command
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously the chatbot only greeted the user and exited immediately,
without reading any input.

Let's add a loop that reads each line of user input and echoes it
back, until the user types "bye", at which point the chatbot prints
the farewell message and exits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add task storage and list command
Chatbot: Add mark and unmark task commands
Add support for ToDos, Deadlines, and Events
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously all user input was stored as a plain string, so the app
could not distinguish between task kinds or attach date/time info.

Add a Task class hierarchy so each task kind owns its own display
logic:

* Task: abstract base holding the description and done status
* Todo: task with no date/time attached
* Deadline: task with a /by date/time
* Event: task with /from and /to date/times

Add a TaskType enum that pairs each kind's command keyword with its
list icon (T, D, E), used for both command dispatch and rendering.

Tasks are now shown as [<type>][<status>] description, with Deadline
and Event appending their date fragment via super.toString(). Adding
a task reports the task and the updated task count.

Dates/times are stored as plain strings; parsing them into real date
objects is left for a later increment.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: fix gradle compatibility
commitResults.messageBody:
build.gradle's application.mainClass was still 'seedu.duke.Duke', the
generic course-template value from the add-gradle-support branch. The
project's actual entry point is Rocky, in the default package on this
branch, so ./gradlew run and the shadow jar's Main-Class couldn't
find it. Point mainClass at 'Rocky' instead.

Verified by compiling src/main/java and running "java -cp <classes>
Rocky", the same invocation Gradle's application plugin and shadow
jar manifest now produce.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Configure Gradle to build executable JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
Rename the shadowJar output from the leftover template name
'duke.jar' to 'rocky.jar', matching this project. The shadow plugin,
application.mainClass = 'Rocky', and the disabled plain jar task were
already set up correctly from the add-gradle-support merge, so this
was the one piece that needed fixing.

Verified by hand: since this sandbox can't reach plugins.gradle.org
or Maven Central to run ./gradlew shadowJar directly, I built an
equivalent jar with the JDK's own jar tool (same classes, same
Main-Class: Rocky manifest entry a shadowJar run would produce),
copied it into an empty folder, and ran it as
`java -jar "rocky.jar"` per the required usage pattern. It started,
greeted, and exited cleanly on "bye".

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add JavaDoc comments
commitResults.messageBody:
Add JavaDoc to every non-private class and method across all seven
source files, plus the non-trivial private helper methods in Rocky
(load/save/parseIndex/taskToLine/lineToTask/ensureDataFile/etc.) -
meeting the stretch goal rather than just the minimal half-coverage
bar. Comments only; no logic changed anywhere.

Verified three ways: javac compiles clean, the javadoc tool runs with
zero warnings (every @param/@return/@throws filled in, including a
private no-arg constructor added to Rocky to silence the "undocumented
default constructor" warning on its all-static utility class), and
the same scripted end-to-end run used throughout this project matches
the pre-change baseline output and save file byte-for-byte.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add assertions to document assumptions
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, several internal assumptions (e.g. a parsed index being
within bounds, a task list never being null, a command word always
being non-empty after splitting) were relied on implicitly, with no
way to catch a violation early if the assumption ever broke.

Let's add Java assert statements at key points across the codebase
to document and check these assumptions, such as: task indices being
within range after parseIndex, the tasks list/count never going
negative, and non-null task objects before printing. Each assertion
is intended to catch programmer errors during development/testing,
not to replace normal exception-based error handling for user input.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Replace magic command-word strings with named constants
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, the command words ("bye", "list", "mark", "unmark",
"delete", "find") were written as bare string literals, and some were
repeated: "bye" was checked separately in getResponse() and
isExitCommand(), and "find" appeared three times in findTasks(). A
typo in any one copy would silently break that command, and renaming
a command meant hunting down every copy.

Let's give each command word a named constant, following the "avoid
magic literals" guideline, and have getResponse() reuse
isExitCommand() so the exit command is defined in exactly one place.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Extract helper for the text after a command word
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, findTasks() and addTask() each extracted the text after
their command word with the same copy-pasted expression:

    input.length() > word.length() ? input.substring(word.length()).trim() : ""

Duplicated logic has to be fixed in every copy if it ever changes, and
the ternary made a simple idea look more complicated than it is.

Let's extract getTextAfterCommand(), following the "minimize code
duplication" and "avoid complicated expressions" guidelines. The
ternary guard isn't needed: substring() at the end of a string already
returns "", so the helper is a single line. The assertion that a line
begins with its command word moves into the helper as well, so it is
stated once rather than in each caller.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Use guard clauses for task-number errors in parseIndex()
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, parseIndex() reported an out-of-range task number with a
single throw whose message was a multi-line ternary choosing between
two different errors (empty list vs. number too large). Readers had
to untangle the ternary to see that there were two separate failure
cases. It also recomputed parts[1].trim() three times.

Let's check each unusual case with its own guard clause that throws
early, following the "avoid complicated expressions" and "make the
happy path prominent" guidelines, and read the number once into a
well-named variable using getTextAfterCommand(). The messages shown
to the user are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Extract shared formatter for numbered task lists
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, listTasks() and findTasks() each built their reply with an
identical copy-pasted loop that numbered the tasks from 1, one per
line. Any change to how a list looks would have to be made twice, and
the two copies could drift apart.

Let's extract formatTaskList(heading, tasks), following the "minimize
code duplication" guideline, so each command only says what it shows
while the way a list is displayed is defined once. The output is
unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Split addTask() into smaller parsing methods
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, addTask() was about 55 lines long, well over the ~30-line
limit the code quality guidelines suggest. It mixed high-level steps
(create a task, add it, save, reply) with low-level string splitting
on " /by ", " /from " and " /to ", so a reader had to wade through
parsing details to see what the method does overall.

Let's move the deadline and event parsing into parseDeadline() and
parseEvent(), following the "avoid long methods" and "SLAP hard"
guidelines. addTask() now reads at a single level of abstraction:
pick the parser for the task type, then add, save, and reply. Error
messages and behavior are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Reject malformed save-file lines instead of guessing or crashing
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, lineToTask() took two unsafe shortcuts. Its switch used
the default branch to treat any unrecognized type letter as a todo,
so a corrupted line such as "X | 0 | foo" was silently loaded as the
wrong kind of task. It also indexed the split fields directly, so a
line with missing fields (e.g. "D | 0 | return book") threw an
uncaught ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException that crashed Rocky on startup,
even though load() is designed to skip unreadable lines with a
warning.

Let's give todos their own "T" case and make the default branch
reject unknown types, following the "use the default branch"
guideline so the unexpected case is handled explicitly. Fields are now
read through getField(), which throws a RockyException when a field
is missing, so load() skips the bad line with its usual warning and
carries on loading the rest of the file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Use TaskType's icons in the save file
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, the save file's type letters "T", "D" and "E" were
hardcoded as string literals in both taskToLine() and lineToTask(),
even though TaskType already defines the same letters through
getIcon(), which nothing called. The letters were duplicated, and
TaskType's icons were effectively dead code that could silently
disagree with what was actually written to disk.

Let's write each task's letter using TaskType.getIcon(), and read it
back with a new TaskType.fromIcon() lookup that mirrors fromKeyword(),
following the "avoid magic literals" and "minimize code duplication"
guidelines. lineToTask() now switches over TaskType values, and an
unknown letter is still rejected. The save-file format itself is
unchanged, so existing saved tasks still load.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Store a task's done state as a plain boolean
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, Task stored its done state in a Boolean object and took it
as a constructor parameter, yet every subclass passed false. The
object type allowed a null that a primitive boolean cannot hold (an
assertion had to guard against it, because isDone() would throw a
NullPointerException when unboxing it), and the always-false parameter
made readers wonder when a task could ever start out done.

Let's use a primitive boolean that starts as false and drop the
parameter, following the "make the code obvious" and "KISS"
guidelines, and the "do not trip up the reader" advice against
parameters that serve no purpose. The null assertion is removed
because a primitive can never be null.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Format all task types consistently
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, the three task types printed themselves slightly
differently: a todo had a space after its type icon ("[T] [ ] read
book") while deadlines and events did not ("[D][ ] ..."), and a
deadline had no space before its date ("return book(by: Dec 01 2019)")
while an event did ("meeting (from: ...)"). Similar things that look
different for no reason trip up the reader, both of the code and of
Rocky's replies.

Let's give every type the same "[X][ ] description (details)" layout,
following the "do not trip up the reader" guideline. Only the
displayed text changes; the save-file format is unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Explain why Launcher exists and update stale comments
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, Launcher's only comment was "A launcher class to
workaround classpath issues", which doesn't say what the issue is, so
the class looks like removable boilerplate. Its public main() also had
no header comment. RockyException's comment still said its messages
are shown "via System.out", which stopped being accurate once the GUI
started showing them in dialog boxes.

Let's state the actual reason for Launcher (Java refuses to start an
Application subclass directly from a JAR that bundles JavaFX), and
describe RockyException's messages as shown by whichever UI is in use,
following the "explain WHAT and WHY, not HOW" and "write to the
reader" guidelines.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
